P1.evidence: No setter suffix on the title and no application or setter notes referenced, so P1a does not apply. The frame ran with a disqualification clause, which is a good variant: 'go over what you're trying to achieve, where you're currently at, see if we can help you make that bridge gap. If we can, I'll take you through how. If we cannot, I'll point you in the right direction, okay?' — but it is three parts, with 'what's in the way' and 'what you need' absent. Agreement was sought via the trailing 'okay?' and given. The open question ran: 'take me through, like, what can we potentially help you with?'

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight all asked and answered directly. Diet was the strongest area — protein intake, whole versus processed food, and takeaway frequency were all probed to a specific answer of three to four times a week. But P2c is the critical failure of this call: health conditions were never asked, and the prospect volunteered the single most important fact unprompted — 'I know I'm 43, I have diabetes' and 'I do take a lot of pills, and I do not like that'. The rep did not follow up on the diabetes, the medication or any hereditary history at any point afterwards. Injuries were asked ('You got some pains and aches here and there?') and produced a shoulder that flares under pressing, but duration and severity were never established. Occupation was volunteered rather than asked. Sleep was never raised despite the prospect working 7-to-7 and night shifts, and daily energy was never asked.

P3.evidence: By far the best-run phase and genuinely good work. The surface layer was covered with a specific focus question and a 1-to-10 mobility scale. The bridge question ran almost verbatim and with real skill, using the prospect's own account against him gently: 'what is the main reason for you that you're like, okay, I actually want to change this right now... even though it doesn't even sound that bad at the moment?' — which surfaced the breakup, the diabetes and the medication. The impact question ran on the jumper his son gave him ('What would that do to your mental state overall?') and again on the new job. The who-else question ran ('You mentioned your son... what's your bigger why?') and drove through to a powerful longevity anchor that the prospect owns himself: staying mobile and not ending up in a nursing home like the residents he cares for. Only the 'something you want to do but can't' question was approximated rather than asked, and the closing recap was an accurate list with a confirmation check rather than the 'this isn't really about the weight' reframe.

P4.evidence: Thin, though partly because there is little history to mine — the prospect has never trained or used a fitness coach. The rep did ask 'have you ever had a coach for anything before?' and established the years of inaction ('how long have you been with that idea... but you haven't actually?' — 'years'). But 'what happened with that?', 'what's the one thing actually getting in the way?' and the 'the information isn't the problem' challenge were all absent. When soliciting the gap the rep asked the right question — 'What would you need to have, like, for you personally, of a coach?' — but the prospect could not answer ('just tell it to me straight as it is') and the rep supplied the answer for him: 'okay, I need accountability, I need the directness'. The prospect then agreed to the rep's framing rather than naming his own gap, so the credit is partial.

P5.evidence: Substantially run, and a clear improvement on the rep's other call the same day. The two-year projection ran properly — 'where do you think that you will be at in a couple of years from now if you don't make those big changes for yourself?' — and produced a genuinely useful admission: 'I would actually stay the same. I'll probably just give up on the outcome. It would just go back to being the same old.' The settle question ran too ('Would that be something that you would be okay with?'). But the answer that came back was contradictory — 'Correction, I would say yes, because it was comfortable' — and instead of pressing 'why not?' into that contradiction, the rep pivoted to a hamburger scenario and an angel-and-devil metaphor that confused the prospect into 'to be truthful, actually, I don't know the actual answer to it.' The line-in-the-sand landed only as a soft 'Is that something you want to do?'.

P6.evidence: Correctly sequenced — the commitment check was run at 00:30:48, before the presentation began at 00:31:24, which is what the script asks for and which the rep did not do on his other call the same day. The belief question ran in full: 'let's say you have that structure for yourself... and someone like Trevor in your corner guiding you through it... Do you feel like you're actually going to be able to follow through?' and produced an unambiguous 'Oh, definitely, yes. Yes.' The all-in isolation question was not asked here — it appeared later, folded into the money play at 00:44:08 — so no blockers were surfaced before the presentation.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and price was presented, so the phase applies, but not one of the four steps completed. No payment was collected — not even the $100 deposit, since the prospect's account was overdrawn. Onboarding with Trevor was explicitly gated behind money: 'Trevor doesn't book like onboarding meetings until we have got one month in.' No agreement email was mentioned and nothing was signed. No welcome email, no Skool link and no onboarding questionnaire; the promised 'homework' was made conditional on Thursday's payment. The call ended with a plan to text rather than any completed step.

objection_plays.detail: Triggered by '6K. Is this something I can break down into payments?' and the run was mechanically the most complete in this batch. Isolation ran first and twice, correctly: 'outside of the investment, do you feel like, yeah, Richard, let's just do this?' The open-conversation permission question ran close to script: 'Let's just have an open conversation about it. you okay with that?' The break-it-up framing ran: 'most guys, they just put on a credit card... When it comes to breaking it up, what would be doable for you?' Cash on hand ran ('What is currently available on your checking?'), as did credit card count ('do you have multiple cards that you usually use?'). Missing: monthly surplus after bills was never asked, available credit per card and used-versus-available were replaced by a single credit-score question, and crypto, stocks and investments were never raised. The 'SHOULD I versus HOW' reframe was not used. The process grade is partial; the judgement issue — that this play was run to completion on a man who had just disclosed an overdrawn account — is recorded in the flags rather than here.

Script gap, and the most consequential one in the corpus so far. The prospect disclosed diabetes managed by multiple daily medications and a shoulder that flares under pressing, both unprompted. The playbook contains no clinical screen, no clearance step and no play for a prospect with an active chronic condition, so nothing in the process required the rep to stop, ask what the medications were, or ask whether a physician had cleared loaded ballistic training. He did not. This is the same structural absence already noted in the ICP observations — that the stated ICP has no clinical criterion — surfacing here as a live safety gap rather than a lost deal.

Second script gap. Objection C assumes the blocker is willingness or liquidity that can be unlocked by structuring. Here the prospect had no capacity at all — overdrawn, no credit cards, a 545 credit score that disqualified him from third-party financing, and no funds until payday. There is no scripted path for disqualifying on affordability with dignity, so the rep improvised downward through a six-part plan, then a first instalment, then a $100 deposit, then a deferral to Thursday, rather than concluding the prospect could not be served.

notes: Genuinely strong discovery — Goals was excellent, the Consequence Frame ran, and the commitment check was correctly placed before the presentation, all of which the rep failed to do on his other call the same day. The failures are of judgement rather than of process. He was handed a diabetes and medication disclosure and did not ask a single follow-up question, and he ran the open-wallet play to its conclusion on a prospect who had disclosed an overdrawn account. Coach on stopping the call to establish clinical clearance when a condition is disclosed, and on treating a disclosed overdraft as a disqualification signal rather than an obstacle to structure around.
